title: More than 15.5 million Australians will have no say in who inherits their superannuation
full_text:
Brooke Allan loved her uncle like a father.
When he died, she thought his superannuation money would be split equally between her and her cousin, as it was their names her uncle had listed on the death benefit nomination form with his super fund, Cbus.
A few months after he died, in February 2024, Ms Allan and her cousin lodged a claim for her uncle's super money, in accordance with his wishes.
Ms Allan said that after repeated phone calls, emails, statutory declarations and several different Cbus case managers, the super fund sent her and her cousin its decision on April 23, 2025.
It turns out, the nomination — for his nieces to inherit his superannuation — was not legally binding.
The fund decided that her uncle's estranged son was the sole beneficiary and awarded him the entire payout, totalling $130,000.
"It's been an emotional rollercoaster," Ms Allan told ABC News.
"I've been very angry because my uncle was my person; he was so special to me."
Superannuation does not automatically form part of a person's estate or pass according to their will, because it is held in a trust managed by a superannuation fund trustee.
As the trustee, the super fund has the discretion to decide who inherits the member's money.
When Ms Allan learned that, she was in shock.
"It's not about the money, it's about the request of someone who is deceased," she said.
"Why do we bother nominating anyone and why do we bother putting our wishes down … if these companies are not going to abide by them?"
Cbus acted in accordance with the law.
But the case shows how complicated the payout process can be when super funds receive claims from multiple family members for a dead person's super.
It also highlights the importance of Australians having a binding death benefit nomination, but it is estimated that more than 15.5 million people have not nominated who inherits their superannuation when they die, according to new research from Super Consumers Australia.
'Funds doing a poor job'
Super Consumers' Your Say on Super national survey asked people with money in super funds whether their fund had, in the past 12 months, encouraged them to make a legally binding death benefit nomination.
The survey of 5,000 people, conducted between August 7 and September 9, 2025, found 67 per cent of people had not been contacted by their fund about making a binding death benefit nomination, while only 10 per cent had, 10 per cent said they could not remember and just 13 per cent said they already had one.
That means 87 per cent of people surveyed reported not having a binding death benefit nomination.
Super Consumers uses ATO data showing there are about 18 million people with a superannuation account.
If the 87 per cent figure is applied to 18 million, that means about 15.7 million people do not have a binding death benefit nomination.
"Funds have been doing a very poor job of letting people know that they have to have one [a binding death benefit nomination] set up," says Super Consumers chief executive Xavier O'Halloran.
"They [super fund members] are completely in the dark about how important these [binding death benefit nominations] are and how to set them up."
The impact can be devastating for the members' loved ones.
"We're talking in some cases years before that money will get paid out to the people that they [the super fund member] loves, when they pass away," Mr O'Halloran said.
"It could also mean the money doesn't go where they want the money to go."
The findings come as the regulator, the Australian Securities Investment Commission (ASIC), ramps up its surveillance of super funds and how long they take to pay out death benefit claims.
The regulator's review of super funds last year found claims with no nomination or a non-binding nomination took the longest to process.
The regulator also has found limited industry-wide progress on speeding up death benefit claims, with a more recent report released in June showing only a 3 per cent improvement in the number completed in under six months.
"ASIC has taken enforcement action against trustees for member service failures," Ms Constant said.
"We will not hesitate to act again to ensure consumers receive the outcomes they deserve.
"Too many grieving families are still waiting too long for payments."
Some death benefit nominations not legally binding
Some superannuation funds do not permit legally binding death benefit nominations, offering only non-binding nominations instead.
ABC News has received correspondence from some members who had emails from their super fund telling them under their policy they were not able to have a binding nomination.
Under current laws, there are strict rules about who can be an eligible "beneficiary", for example, a partner, child or someone who is financially dependent.
A member may also nominate a legal personal representative as a beneficiary.
As Ms Allan discovered, the super fund has total discretion to decide who the beneficiary is.
In its decision letter to Ms Allan and her cousin, Cbus said while the fund "acknowledges the nomination on the member's account from August 2019 for his death benefit to be equally apportioned (50/50) to Brooke Allan and [her cousin], the Trustee is not bound by the nomination but uses it as a guide having regard to the member's wishes".
It said while "the late member may have had a close relationship with Brooke and [her cousin], that does not make them dependent on him in accordance with superannuation legislation or the rules of the fund".
"While we acknowledge there is some information which supports the late member provided Brooke and [her cousin] with sporadic financial assistance at points in time of hardship, these do not appear to be regular and ongoing," the letter continued.
"The trustee has, however, only been able to identify the late member's son as the only dependant."
ABC News attempted to contact the member's son through his lawyers, but he declined to comment.
A Cbus Super spokesman apologised to Ms Allan for the delays in determining the death benefit claim.
"While we must always meet our legal obligations, we are sorry if previous processes caused delays or added complications for members and their families," he said.
He told ABC News that more recently the fund "has undertaken significant reforms to simplify its death and insurance claims processes, aimed at providing greater certainty, clarity about who will receive the benefit, and faster support for families during difficult times".
"Early results show the new approach is helping us pay claims substantially faster," the spokesman said.
Ms Allan said the whole process of making a death benefit claim had been emotionally taxing.
"So many Australians have no idea what happens to their super or what goes on behind the scenes — they have no idea about the control these super companies have in dictating where their hard-earned money goes," she said.
"Sometimes I feel like, it's better off we just keep our money under mattress."
Ms Allan would like to see the law changed so that Australians can nominate who their super goes to as part of their will, rather than give super funds the discretion about who they pay out.
Death benefit nominations can lapse
Martin Corden also wants to see the law changed so that who inherits your super can be paid out as part of whoever you list in your will, rather than rely on super funds to decide.
Upon reading ABC News's previous article on death benefit nominations, Mr Corden did some research and discovered his nomination was not binding.
He also learned that death benefit nominations are not forever. They generally lapse every few years.
"I don't understand why they make it so cumbersome," he told ABC News.
"I was alarmed when I discovered that the balance of your super fund upon your death is not considered part of your estate and thus is outside of the will. I simply don't understand why that is because it imposes this burden upon every superannuation member."
Mr Corden said the government should change the rules so that who you leave your super to can be part of your will, without the need for a separate binding nomination with your super fund's trustee.
"I do think superannuation funds, in the meantime, could make the process simpler and clearer by firstly removing the whole concept of non-binding nominations, because it seems entirely pointless, and secondly making all binding nominations perpetual and that they don't lapse after three years," he said.
He said he had set up a non-lapsing binding nomination with his fund, AustralianSuper.
An AustralianSuper spokesperson told ABC News: "We are digitising the process members use to make non-lapsing nominations of beneficiaries, to make it easier for them to tell us where they want their money to go after they die.
"Under current regulations, lapsing nomination forms require physical signatures — we've called since 2024 for these laws to be updated."
Super funds vow to do better
But super funds are not always reminding members to make nominations and check their nominations are up to date.
The regulator, ASIC, found most trustees only contacted the member once before their nomination expired, and some sent notices one day before the nomination lapsed.
It also found that very few funds regularly "nudged" or prompted members to make binding nominations, or periodically ran proactive nomination campaigns.
ASIC's Simone Constant said funds "must be more proactive, rather than relying on passive communication through annual statements".
Misha Schubert is chief executive of the Super Members Council, formerly Industry Super Australia, which represents industry funds.
She said many super funds were working hard to ensure members can easily set up a binding death benefit nomination.
"At the moment the law requires that [signatures] to be done on a hard copy paper form with two wet ink signatures — for a lot of people they look at that and they think 'it's 2026!'" she said.
Ms Schubert said people could file tax returns or sign contracts via secured digital portals, and so "the same broad processes should be able to be adopted for people to be able to make a binding death nomination".
"What we can see across the system, there's been significant efforts across the last couple of years in particular to try to lift those levels of member awareness, but there's much more that can be done," Ms Schubert said.
She also believes that all super funds should allow members to make legally binding death benefit nominations.
Calls for mandatory timeframes for super funds to respond to claims
The federal government is considering whether to change the law to include mandatory timeframes for super funds to respond to insurance claims, including death benefit claims.
Mr O'Halloran from Super Consumers Australia thinks mandatory timeframes are needed to speed up payouts.
"Superannuation funds have been pushing back on what's called an end-to-end timeframe," he said.
"That's a timeframe from when you first make an application or first contact the super fund about making an application, right through to when the money's paid out.
"We want to see those as tight as possible to make sure people aren't waiting forever to get the money that's owed to them."
But Ms Schubert said, while the Super Members Council was in favour of better customer service standards, mandatory timeframes should not apply to complex cases.
"For instance, if you've got … someone who's got multiple families because they've been in multiple relationships and there are multiple children from those relationships."
She said in those cases trustees must "weigh carefully the claims of multiple people who have a stake potentially", and that this could take time.
